summary: At the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus fills an empty net, gives His disciples breakfast, and restores Peter with three questions and a call to feed His sheep.
key_insight: When the disciples reached the shore, fish was already cooking on the fire. Jesus did not need their catch, yet He said, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.” He fed them from His own provision and still made room for what their work had brought in.
story: After these things Jesus showed Himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. Seven of them were together: Simon Peter, Thomas called the Twin, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee and two others. Peter said, “I am going fishing,” and the others went with him. That night they caught nothing.

At daybreak Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not know it was He. He called, “Children, have you any food?” “No,” they answered. “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” They did, and now they could not draw it in because of the multitude of fish.

The disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” Peter put on his outer garment, which he had taken off, and plunged into the sea. The others came in the little boat, about a hundred yards from land, dragging the net full of fish.

On the shore they saw a fire of coals with fish laid on it, and bread. Jesus said, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.” Peter dragged the net to land, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three, and the net was not broken. “Come and eat breakfast,” Jesus said. None of them dared ask Him, “Who are You?” They knew it was the Lord. He took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish as well. This was the third time Jesus showed Himself to His disciples after He was raised from the dead.

When they had eaten, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me more than these?” “Yes, Lord; You know that I love You.” “Feed My lambs.” A second time He asked, and Peter answered the same, and Jesus said, “Tend My sheep.” When Jesus asked the third time, Peter was grieved and said, “Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep.”

Then Jesus told Peter that when he was young he dressed himself and went where he wished, “but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish.” He said this to show by what death Peter would glorify God. Then He said to him, “Follow Me.”

Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who had leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper. “But Lord, what about this man?” Jesus answered, “If I will that he remain till I come, what is that to you? You follow Me.” A saying went out among the brethren that this disciple would not die, but Jesus had not said that. This is the disciple who testifies of these things and wrote them, and his testimony is true. There are also many other things that Jesus did. If they were all written one by one, “I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.”

scene.label: The Sea of Tiberias
scene.text: This is John’s name for the Sea of Galilee (also John 6:1). Herod Antipas built the city of Tiberias on its western shore about AD 20 and named it for the emperor Tiberius, and in time the lake took the city’s name.

scene.label: Two hundred cubits
scene.text: A cubit was about a foot and a half, so the boat was about a hundred yards out, close enough to hear a voice calling from the beach.

scene.label: One hundred and fifty-three
scene.text: John gives the exact count, the kind of detail men remember after hauling in and counting a catch. Many symbolic meanings have been suggested over the centuries. John offers none; his point is that the catch was huge and the net held.

scene.label: Two words for love
scene.text: In Greek, Jesus’ first two questions use the verb agapao, and Peter answers each time with phileo; the third time Jesus uses Peter’s word. Some see a deliberate change. Others note that John uses both verbs for the Father’s love of the Son (John 3:35; 5:20). Either way, the third asking is what grieved Peter.

scene.label: “Stretch out your hands”
scene.text: Early Christians understood these words as pointing to crucifixion. Church tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero in the 60s. Peter later wrote that his death was near, “just as our Lord Jesus Christ showed me” (2 Peter 1:14).

witnesses.john: John alone records this morning, in a closing chapter that follows what had sounded like the end of his Gospel (20:30–31) and ends with a wider close still: the world itself could not contain the books (21:25). It restores Peter in front of the others and corrects a rumor that the beloved disciple would not die before Jesus came. John counts it the third time Jesus showed Himself to the disciples as a group (21:14), after the two Sunday evenings in Jerusalem.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is Lord of the catch and Host of the meal. He restores His fallen disciple not by reviewing the failure but by asking about his love and giving him sheep to feed.
seeing.living: Before Peter could feed anyone, he had to answer one question: “Do you love Me?” And when he looked over at John to compare, Jesus turned him back: “You follow Me.” Love for Jesus, not comparison with other believers, fits a servant for the work He gives.
seeing.ponder: If Jesus asked you by name today, “Do you love Me?”, how would you honestly answer, and whom might He be asking you to feed?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus restores failures by asking for their love and giving them His sheep to feed.
outline: Empty nets and a word from the shore (1–8)
Three questions for a fallen disciple (15–17)
preaching.watch_for: Two echoes open the passage. The “fire of coals” appears elsewhere only at Peter’s denial (18:18), and three questions answer three denials. The catch recalls Peter’s first call by the same lake (Luke 5:1–11), and the morning ends with the words of that first call, “Follow Me” (21:19, 22; Mark 1:17).
